An aerie is the nest of a large bird of prey — most commonly an eagle, but also hawks, falcons, and ospreys. What makes an aerie special and different from a typical bird's nest is where it is built: always very high up — on the edge of a steep cliff, on a rocky mountain ledge, or at the very top of a tall, isolated tree.

Think of it this way: if a robin's nest is like a small cozy apartment on the ground floor, an aerie is a fortress penthouse at the very top of a skyscraper. It is always up high, hard to reach, and commanding.
What an Aerie Actually Looks Like

An aerie is not the delicate, cup-shaped nest you might picture when you think of birds. It is large, heavy, and built to last. Eagles, for example, construct their aeries out of thick sticks, branches, and twigs, and then line the inside with softer materials — grass, moss, leaves, or feathers — to cushion the eggs and chicks.

Aeries are also reused year after year. A pair of eagles will return to the same aerie every breeding season and add more material to it each time. Over many years, an aerie can grow enormous — some bald eagle aeries have been recorded weighing over a ton and measuring nearly 10 feet across. This makes the aerie feel less like a temporary nest and more like a permanent home.

The height of an aerie is not accidental — it is the whole point. There are three key reasons large birds of prey nest so high:

  1. Safety from predators. Most ground predators — foxes, raccoons, snakes — simply cannot reach a nest perched on a sheer cliff face or at the very crown of a tall tree. The height is a natural defense.
  2. A wide view of the surrounding landscape. From a high aerie, the parent birds can spot threats approaching from a great distance. They can also scan vast areas of land below for prey.
  3. Easy launching for flight. Large birds with wide wingspans need open, unobstructed space to take off. A high ledge or treetop gives them a perfect launching pad — they can simply drop off the edge and spread their wings into the air currents below.

So the aerie is not just a nest — it is a strategically chosen, defensible, high-altitude home base.

The word is most strongly associated with eagles, but it applies to any large bird of prey that nests in a high, elevated place. This includes:

  • Eagles (bald eagles, golden eagles)
  • Hawks (red-tailed hawks, for example)
  • Ospreys
  • Falcons (peregrine falcons famously nest on cliff ledges, and in modern cities, on tall building ledges and bridges)
  • Occasionally, large owls

Smaller birds do not build aeries. The word carries the sense of something large, powerful, and majestic — a bird that rules the skies and picks a home that reflects that dominance.

Because of its association with great height and lofty isolation, the word aerie is also used figuratively to describe any human dwelling, room, or place that is perched very high up or feels remote and elevated from the world below.

For example:

  • A penthouse apartment on the 80th floor of a skyscraper could be called an aerie.
  • A remote mountain cabin far above a valley could be described as someone's aerie.
  • A writer who retreats to a tiny room at the top of a tower to work in solitude might call it their aerie.

In all these figurative uses, the same core idea carries through: high up, isolated, with a commanding view, away from the ordinary world below.

You may also see this word spelled eyrie (especially in British English). Both spellings refer to exactly the same thing and are equally correct. "Aerie" is more common in American English; "eyrie" is more common in British English.

• The golden eagle returned to its aerie on the cliff each spring to lay eggs.
  • From her aerie at the top of the old lighthouse, she could see for miles in every direction.
  • The young eaglets were too small to leave the aerie yet, so the mother kept watch nearby.
  • The billionaire's glass aerie — his penthouse fifty stories above the city — made him feel untouchable.

An aerie is the large, sturdy nest of a bird of prey, always built in a very high, hard-to-reach place like a cliff or a mountaintop — and by extension, any elevated, isolated retreat that feels similarly lofty and remote.
